stem: A student looks at a labelled diagram of an animal cell. Which structure is present in animal cells but NOT in plant cells?

options.text: Cell wall
options.misconception_tag: thinks the cell wall is animal-specific, confusing it with the cell membrane

options.text: Mitochondria
options.misconception_tag: thinks mitochondria are only in animal cells because animals are more active

options.text: There is no structure unique to animal cells; plant cells contain all the structures an animal cell has, plus extra ones (cell wall, chloroplasts, vacuole).
Ribosomes
options.misconception_tag: thinks ribosomes are only found in animal cells

stem: Which structure controls what substances enter and leave the cell?

options.text: The cell wall
options.misconception_tag: confuses the cell wall (support) with the membrane (controlling movement)

options.text: The cell membrane
The cytoplasm
options.misconception_tag: thinks the jelly-like cytoplasm regulates entry/exit of substances

options.text: The nucleus
options.misconception_tag: thinks the nucleus controls movement of substances because it 'controls the cell'

stem: A bacterial cell is examined. Which feature shows it is a prokaryotic cell rather than a eukaryotic cell?

options.text: It has a cell membrane surrounding the cytoplasm.
options.misconception_tag: thinks having a membrane distinguishes prokaryotes, but both cell types have one

options.text: Its genetic material is not enclosed in a nucleus.
It contains no genetic material at all.
options.misconception_tag: thinks prokaryotes have no DNA, rather than DNA that is free in the cytoplasm

options.text: It has no ribosomes, so it cannot make proteins.
options.misconception_tag: thinks prokaryotes lack ribosomes, when they do contain them

stem: What is the function of the mitochondria in a cell?

options.text: They are the site of most respiration reactions, transferring energy for the cell.
They make energy for the cell out of nothing.
options.misconception_tag: thinks mitochondria create/produce energy rather than transfer it by respiration

options.text: They are the site of photosynthesis to make glucose.
options.misconception_tag: confuses mitochondria with chloroplasts

options.text: They control the activities of the cell and contain the DNA.
options.misconception_tag: confuses the role of mitochondria with that of the nucleus

stem: Why are chloroplasts found in the cells of a plant's leaves but NOT usually in the cells of its roots?

options.text: Root cells do not receive light, so chloroplasts there could not carry out photosynthesis.
Roots do not need energy, so they have no need for chloroplasts.
options.misconception_tag: thinks roots do not respire/need energy, and confuses chloroplast role with energy supply generally

options.text: Chloroplasts would be damaged by the water in the soil.
options.misconception_tag: invents a damage mechanism rather than reasoning about light availability

options.text: Root cells are too small to contain chloroplasts.
options.misconception_tag: thinks organelle presence is limited by cell size rather than function

stem: An electron microscope is used instead of a light microscope to study a cell. What is the main advantage of the electron microscope?

options.text: It has a higher resolving power, so smaller sub-cellular structures can be seen clearly.
It magnifies the image, whereas a light microscope cannot magnify at all.
options.misconception_tag: thinks light microscopes do not magnify, confusing magnification with resolution

options.text: It can be used to view living, moving cells in colour.
options.misconception_tag: thinks electron microscopes show living cells in natural colour

options.text: It makes the cell bigger in real life so it is easier to handle.
options.misconception_tag: thinks magnification physically enlarges the specimen

stem: What is the function of ribosomes in a cell?

options.text: Protein synthesis.
Respiration to release energy.
options.misconception_tag: confuses ribosomes with mitochondria

options.text: Storing the genetic information of the cell.
options.misconception_tag: confuses ribosomes with the nucleus/DNA

options.text: Controlling what enters and leaves the cell.
options.misconception_tag: confuses ribosomes with the cell membrane

stem: A cheek cell is 0.06 mm long. The same cell measured in an image is 60 mm long. What is the magnification of the image?

options.misconception_tag: divides real size by image size instead of image size by real size
makes a unit/place-value error when dividing 60 by 0.06
uses only the image size and ignores the real size in the calculation

stem: Why is a sperm cell described as a specialised cell?

options.text: It is adapted, with features such as a tail and many mitochondria, to carry out one particular function.
It is a completely different type of cell that is not really made of the same parts as other cells.
options.misconception_tag: thinks specialised cells are not built from the same basic cell structure

options.text: It can change into any other type of cell whenever the body needs it.
options.misconception_tag: confuses a specialised cell with a stem cell

options.text: It is the only cell in the body that contains a nucleus.
options.misconception_tag: thinks only specialised reproductive cells have a nucleus

stem: Which structure is found in BOTH a plant cell and a bacterial cell?

options.text: Cell membrane
Chloroplast
options.misconception_tag: thinks bacteria photosynthesise using chloroplasts like plant cells

options.text: Nucleus
options.misconception_tag: thinks bacteria have a true nucleus like plant cells

options.text: Permanent vacuole
options.misconception_tag: thinks bacterial cells contain a large permanent vacuole like plant cells

stem: What does the cell wall of a plant cell do, and what is it mainly made of?

options.text: It strengthens and supports the cell, and is made mainly of cellulose.
It controls what enters and leaves the cell, and is made of cellulose.
options.misconception_tag: gives the cell membrane's function to the cell wall

options.text: It supports the cell and is made mainly of fat (lipid).
options.misconception_tag: confuses the cellulose wall with the lipid membrane composition

options.text: It stops all substances passing through, making the cell completely sealed.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the cell wall is impermeable, when it is freely permeable

stem: Where in a eukaryotic cell is the chromosomal DNA found?

options.text: Enclosed within the nucleus.
Free in the cytoplasm.
options.misconception_tag: applies the prokaryotic arrangement of DNA to a eukaryotic cell

options.text: Inside the mitochondria only.
options.misconception_tag: thinks all of a cell's DNA is stored in mitochondria

options.text: Attached to the inside of the cell membrane.
options.misconception_tag: thinks DNA is held on the cell membrane

stem: A student writes that 'a bacterial cell is much smaller than an animal cell'. Which comparison of typical sizes supports this statement?

options.text: A bacterial cell is a few micrometres across, while an animal cell is tens of micrometres across.
A bacterial cell is a few millimetres across, while an animal cell is a few micrometres across.
options.misconception_tag: reverses the scale, thinking bacteria are larger than animal cells

options.text: Both are about the same size, but bacteria only look smaller under the microscope.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the apparent size difference is only due to magnification, not real size

options.text: A bacterial cell is measured in nanometres, the same units used for an animal cell.
options.misconception_tag: confuses the appropriate units of scale for cells (nm vs micrometres)

stem: Which statement correctly describes diffusion?

options.text: The net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration, down a concentration gradient.
The movement of particles from a lower to a higher concentration using energy from respiration.
options.misconception_tag: confuses diffusion with active transport / thinks diffusion is against the gradient

options.text: The movement of water only across a partially permeable membrane.
options.misconception_tag: confuses diffusion with osmosis and restricts it to water

options.text: The movement of particles that continues only until all particles are on one side.
options.misconception_tag: thinks diffusion stops when particles are separated rather than evenly spread

stem: A few drops of perfume are released in one corner of a still, sealed room. After some time the smell can be detected everywhere. What best explains why the diffusion eventually appears to stop?

options.text: The perfume particles become evenly spread, so there is no longer a concentration gradient and no net movement.
The perfume particles stop moving completely once they are spread out.
options.misconception_tag: thinks particles become stationary at equilibrium rather than continuing random motion

options.text: All the perfume particles move to the opposite corner of the room.
options.misconception_tag: thinks diffusion moves all particles fully to the other side

options.text: The perfume particles are used up by the air in the room.
options.misconception_tag: thinks diffusing particles are consumed or destroyed

stem: Which of the following is an example of a substance moving by diffusion in the human body?

options.text: Oxygen moving from the alveoli into the blood in the lungs.
Mineral ions moving from the soil into root hair cells against the gradient.
options.misconception_tag: thinks uptake against a gradient is diffusion rather than active transport

options.text: Water moving from dilute urine into the blood across the kidney tubule.
options.misconception_tag: labels water movement across a membrane as diffusion instead of osmosis

options.text: Glucose being pumped from the gut into the blood when gut concentration is lower.
options.misconception_tag: thinks movement against a concentration gradient is diffusion

stem: Two identical agar cubes are placed in coloured dye. Cube A is 1 cm on each side and cube B is 2 cm on each side. In which cube will the dye diffuse to the centre fastest, and why?

options.text: Cube A, because it has a larger surface area to volume ratio so diffusion distances are shorter relative to its size.
Cube B, because it has a larger surface area so more dye can enter overall.
options.misconception_tag: considers total surface area but ignores volume / surface area to volume ratio

options.text: Cube B, because larger objects always absorb substances faster.
options.misconception_tag: thinks larger size always means faster uptake

options.text: Both at exactly the same rate, because they are made of the same material.
options.misconception_tag: thinks rate depends only on material, not on size or surface area to volume ratio

stem: Which of the following changes would INCREASE the rate of diffusion of oxygen into a cell?

options.text: Increasing the temperature, so particles move faster.
Decreasing the surface area of the cell membrane.
options.misconception_tag: thinks reducing surface area speeds up diffusion

options.text: Increasing the distance the oxygen has to travel.
options.misconception_tag: thinks a longer diffusion path increases the rate

options.text: Reducing the concentration gradient by raising oxygen inside the cell.
options.misconception_tag: thinks a smaller concentration gradient speeds up diffusion

stem: Why do the alveoli in the lungs have a very large surface area and walls only one cell thick?

options.text: To increase the rate of diffusion of gases by providing a large area and a short diffusion distance.
To increase the rate of osmosis of water into the air spaces.
options.misconception_tag: thinks gas exchange in the lungs is osmosis

options.text: To use less energy when actively transporting oxygen into the blood.
options.misconception_tag: thinks gas exchange in the lungs is active transport requiring energy

options.text: To slow down the loss of oxygen so it stays in the lungs longer.
options.misconception_tag: thinks adaptations are to slow rather than speed up exchange

stem: Single-celled organisms such as Amoeba can rely on diffusion alone to obtain oxygen, but large multicellular animals cannot. Which statement best explains this?

options.text: Single-celled organisms have a large surface area to volume ratio and short diffusion distances, so diffusion alone meets their needs.
Single-celled organisms do not need oxygen because they do not respire.
options.misconception_tag: thinks single-celled organisms do not respire

options.text: Large animals have a larger surface area to volume ratio, so they cannot lose oxygen fast enough.
options.misconception_tag: reverses the surface area to volume ratio relationship with size

options.text: Diffusion only works in water, so land animals must use other methods.
options.misconception_tag: thinks diffusion cannot occur in air/across membranes on land

stem: In which direction will carbon dioxide diffuse between a respiring muscle cell and the surrounding blood?

options.text: Out of the muscle cell into the blood, because respiration makes carbon dioxide concentration higher inside the cell.
Into the muscle cell from the blood, because cells always take in carbon dioxide.
options.misconception_tag: assumes a fixed direction of movement rather than following the gradient

options.text: There is no movement, because carbon dioxide cannot pass through cell membranes.
options.misconception_tag: thinks gases cannot diffuse across the cell membrane

options.text: Out of the muscle cell, but only because it is actively pumped out using energy.
options.misconception_tag: thinks carbon dioxide removal is active transport, not diffusion

stem: Which property of a cell membrane allows oxygen and carbon dioxide to diffuse across it?

options.text: It is partially permeable, allowing small molecules like oxygen and carbon dioxide to pass through.
It is fully permeable, so any substance of any size can pass through freely.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the membrane lets all substances through regardless of size

options.text: It is completely impermeable, so substances pass through gaps where the membrane is broken.
options.misconception_tag: thinks diffusion needs a damaged or broken membrane

options.text: It actively grabs gas molecules and carries them across using energy.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the membrane uses energy to move gases by diffusion

stem: A student says: 'If you double the concentration difference across a membrane, the rate of diffusion stays the same.' Which statement is correct?

options.text: The student is wrong; a steeper concentration gradient increases the rate of diffusion.
The student is correct; the concentration gradient has no effect on diffusion rate.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the concentration gradient does not affect diffusion rate

options.text: The student is wrong; a steeper concentration gradient decreases the rate of diffusion.
options.misconception_tag: thinks a bigger gradient slows diffusion down

options.text: The student is correct, because diffusion only depends on temperature.
options.misconception_tag: thinks temperature is the only factor affecting diffusion rate

stem: Which of the following best describes the movement of the individual particles during diffusion?

options.text: Particles move randomly in all directions, but there is a net movement down the concentration gradient.
Every particle moves in a straight line directly from high to low concentration.
options.misconception_tag: thinks particles move in a directed straight line rather than randomly

options.text: Particles only move when they are pushed by an outside force.
options.misconception_tag: thinks particles need an external push and do not move on their own

options.text: Particles move from low to high concentration to fill empty spaces.
options.misconception_tag: thinks net movement is up the concentration gradient to fill 'gaps'

stem: The lining of the small intestine is folded into millions of tiny villi. How does this adaptation help diffusion of digested food into the blood?

options.text: It increases the surface area, so more molecules can diffuse across in a given time.
It decreases the surface area, so food is absorbed more gently.
options.misconception_tag: thinks folding reduces surface area

options.text: It increases the distance food must travel, giving more time to be absorbed.
options.misconception_tag: thinks a longer diffusion distance helps absorption

options.text: It allows food to be absorbed by osmosis instead of diffusion.
options.misconception_tag: confuses absorption of dissolved food molecules with osmosis

stem: A fish gill has a rich blood supply that constantly carries away absorbed oxygen. How does this help diffusion?

options.text: It keeps the oxygen concentration in the blood low, maintaining a steep concentration gradient.
It removes the concentration gradient so diffusion can happen more easily.
options.misconception_tag: thinks removing the gradient speeds up diffusion

options.text: It actively pulls oxygen across the gill using energy from the blood.
options.misconception_tag: thinks a good blood supply means oxygen is actively transported

options.text: It warms the gill so the oxygen molecules dissolve and stop moving.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the purpose is heating and that warming stops particle movement

stem: Which statement correctly compares diffusion and active transport?

options.text: Diffusion moves particles down a concentration gradient without energy, whereas active transport moves them against the gradient using energy from respiration.
Both diffusion and active transport require energy from respiration to occur.
options.misconception_tag: thinks diffusion requires energy like active transport

options.text: Diffusion moves particles up the gradient, while active transport moves them down the gradient.
options.misconception_tag: reverses the gradient directions of diffusion and active transport

options.text: Diffusion only moves water, while active transport only moves dissolved solutes.
options.misconception_tag: confuses diffusion with osmosis and misclassifies the substances moved

stem: Which statement is the most complete and correct definition of osmosis?

options.text: The diffusion of any small molecule from a high to a low concentration across a membrane.
options.misconception_tag: confuses osmosis with general diffusion of solutes

options.text: The net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane.
The active movement of water across a membrane using energy released by respiration.
options.misconception_tag: thinks osmosis requires energy / is active transport

options.text: The movement of water from a region where there is less water to a region where there is more water.
options.misconception_tag: reverses the direction of water movement (high to low water concentration)

stem: A piece of potato is placed in a concentrated sugar solution. After 30 minutes its mass has decreased. What is the best explanation?

options.text: Water left the potato cells by osmosis because the solution had a lower water potential than the cells.
Sugar molecules moved into the potato cells by osmosis, making it heavier inside but lighter overall.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the solute (sugar) moves by osmosis rather than water

options.text: Water entered the potato cells because they started with less water than the solution.
options.misconception_tag: reverses direction of net water movement in a hypertonic solution

options.text: The potato respired, using up its stored glucose and losing mass.
options.misconception_tag: attributes osmotic mass loss to respiration

stem: Red blood cells are placed in pure (distilled) water. What is most likely to happen and why?

options.text: They shrink, because water moves out of the cells into the pure water.
options.misconception_tag: reverses water direction; thinks cells lose water in pure water

options.text: Nothing happens, because pure water contains no solutes to drive osmosis.
options.misconception_tag: thinks osmosis needs solute on both sides / no movement without solutes outside

options.text: They burst (lyse), because water moves into the cells by osmosis and they have no cell wall to resist swelling.
They become turgid but do not burst, because the cell wall stops them swelling too much.
options.misconception_tag: thinks animal cells have a cell wall like plant cells

stem: In an osmosis experiment, why is it important to use a partially permeable membrane rather than a fully permeable one?

options.text: A partially permeable membrane lets water molecules through but blocks larger solute molecules, so a net movement of water can occur.
A partially permeable membrane lets solutes through but blocks water, which is what creates the concentration difference.
options.misconception_tag: reverses what the membrane allows through (water vs solute)

options.text: A fully permeable membrane would stop all movement, so no osmosis could take place.
options.misconception_tag: thinks a fully permeable membrane blocks movement

options.text: A partially permeable membrane uses energy to select which molecules pass, controlling osmosis.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the membrane actively selects molecules using energy

stem: A plant cell is placed in a solution with a HIGHER water potential than the cell. Which term best describes the cell after a while, and why?

options.text: Turgid, because water enters by osmosis and pushes the membrane against the cell wall.
Plasmolysed, because water enters and pulls the membrane away from the wall.
options.misconception_tag: confuses turgid with plasmolysed / wrong water direction

options.text: Flaccid, because the cell wall bursts when water rushes in.
options.misconception_tag: thinks plant cells burst like animal cells

options.text: Lysed, because the cell takes in water until the membrane breaks open.
options.misconception_tag: thinks plant cells lyse; ignores the supporting cell wall

stem: Two solutions are separated by a partially permeable membrane. Solution X is 5% sugar; solution Y is 15% sugar. In which direction does the NET movement of water occur?

options.text: From Y to X, because Y has more sugar so water is attracted towards the sugar.
options.misconception_tag: thinks water is 'attracted' to higher solute via incorrect reasoning

options.text: From X to Y, because X has a higher water potential than Y.
No net movement, because both solutions contain sugar.
options.misconception_tag: thinks any solute on both sides means no osmosis

options.text: From Y to X, because water always moves from a more concentrated to a less concentrated solution.
options.misconception_tag: applies solute-diffusion direction (high to low solute) to water

stem: A student leaves a stick of celery in salty water overnight and it becomes limp and floppy. Why?

options.text: Salt moved into the celery cells by osmosis, making them heavy and limp.
options.misconception_tag: thinks salt (solute) moves by osmosis instead of water

options.text: Water moved out of the celery cells by osmosis because the salty water had a lower water potential, so the cells lost turgor.
Water moved into the celery cells, making them swell and go floppy.
options.misconception_tag: reverses water direction in a hypertonic (salty) solution

options.text: The salt killed the cells, so they could no longer hold water at all.
options.misconception_tag: attributes limpness to cell death rather than osmotic water loss

stem: In a potato-in-sugar-solution experiment, why should each potato cylinder be dried with a paper towel before its final mass is measured?

options.text: To remove surface liquid so it does not add extra mass and give a falsely high reading.
To stop further osmosis from happening while the potato is on the balance.
options.misconception_tag: thinks drying the surface halts osmosis inside the tissue

options.text: To remove sugar that has soaked into the potato and would add mass.
options.misconception_tag: thinks sugar enters the potato by osmosis and must be removed

options.text: To make sure all the water has left the potato before weighing.
options.misconception_tag: confuses removing surface water with removing internal water

stem: At what concentration of sugar solution is the percentage change in mass of a potato cylinder expected to be ZERO?

options.text: At 0% (pure water), because there is no sugar to draw water out.
options.misconception_tag: thinks zero change happens in pure water

options.text: At the concentration where the solution and the potato cells have the SAME water potential, so there is no net movement of water.
At the highest concentration tested, because the solution and potato are both very concentrated.
options.misconception_tag: thinks equilibrium occurs at maximum concentration

options.text: At any concentration, because osmosis only changes shape, never mass.
options.misconception_tag: thinks osmosis does not change the mass of tissue

stem: How does osmosis differ from active transport in the movement of substances across a membrane?

options.text: Osmosis moves water down a water-potential gradient without energy, whereas active transport moves substances against their gradient using energy from respiration.
Osmosis uses energy from respiration, while active transport happens passively down a gradient.
options.misconception_tag: swaps which process uses energy

options.text: Osmosis moves dissolved solutes, while active transport moves only water.
options.misconception_tag: thinks osmosis moves solutes and active transport moves water

options.text: Both move substances from low to high concentration, but only osmosis needs a membrane.
options.misconception_tag: thinks osmosis moves water up the gradient like active transport

stem: Root hair cells absorb water from the soil by osmosis. Which condition makes this possible?

options.text: The soil water has a higher water potential than the cytoplasm of the root hair cell.
The root hair cell actively pumps water in using ATP from respiration.
options.misconception_tag: thinks water uptake into roots is active transport

options.text: The soil water contains more dissolved minerals than the root hair cell, so water follows the minerals in.
options.misconception_tag: thinks water follows solutes / soil is more concentrated

options.text: The root hair cell has a lower water potential because water always moves to where there is less water.
options.misconception_tag: states the principle wrongly as water moving 'to where there is less water' rather than down a water-potential gradient

stem: A visking-tubing bag containing concentrated sugar solution is placed in a beaker of pure water. After 20 minutes the bag has swollen. Why?

options.text: Water moved out of the bag into the pure water, but the tubing trapped air and expanded.
options.misconception_tag: reverses water direction; invents an alternative mechanism

options.text: Sugar diffused out of the bag, pulling water in behind it and swelling the bag.
options.misconception_tag: thinks sugar diffuses through visking tubing and 'pulls' water

options.text: Water moved into the bag by osmosis because the sugar solution had a lower water potential than the surrounding pure water.
The sugar reacted with the water and produced more liquid, increasing the volume.
options.misconception_tag: thinks a chemical reaction produces extra liquid

stem: A potato cylinder in pure water gains 8% in mass, but an identical cylinder in 1.0 mol/dm³ sugar solution loses 12% in mass. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: The 1.0 mol/dm³ solution had a lower water potential than the potato cells, so water left the cells by osmosis.
The 1.0 mol/dm³ solution had a higher water potential than the cells, so water entered them.
options.misconception_tag: reverses the water-potential comparison for a concentrated solution

options.text: Sugar molecules left the potato in the concentrated solution, causing the loss in mass.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the solute leaves the tissue rather than water

options.text: The pure water was warmer, so the cylinder in it expanded and gained mass.
options.misconception_tag: attributes osmotic mass change to thermal expansion

stem: Why do animal cells need careful control of the water concentration in their surroundings, while plant cells can survive in pure water?

options.text: Animal cells respire faster, so they lose water more quickly than plant cells.
options.misconception_tag: links osmotic vulnerability to respiration rate rather than the cell wall

options.text: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall that resists swelling, so they become turgid but do not burst, whereas animal cells have no wall and would lyse.
Plant cells do not take in water by osmosis, so their volume never changes.
options.misconception_tag: thinks plant cells do not undergo osmosis

options.text: Animal cells have a partially permeable membrane but plant cells do not, so only animal cells let water in.
options.misconception_tag: thinks plant cells lack a partially permeable membrane

stem: Which statement correctly describes active transport across a cell membrane?

options.text: The movement of particles from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration, using energy from respiration.
The movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration, using energy from respiration.
options.misconception_tag: reverses the concentration gradient direction; describes facilitated diffusion but adds energy

options.text: The net movement of water from a higher to a lower water potential through a membrane.
options.misconception_tag: confuses active transport with osmosis

options.text: The movement of particles down a concentration gradient without needing any energy.
options.misconception_tag: confuses active transport with simple diffusion

stem: A root hair cell absorbs mineral ions from the soil even though the ion concentration is already higher inside the cell than in the soil. Which process is responsible and why?

options.text: Diffusion, because particles always move into cells from the soil.
options.misconception_tag: thinks diffusion can move particles against a gradient / always inward

options.text: Active transport, because ions are moved against the concentration gradient using energy from respiration.
Osmosis, because the ions follow the water into the cell.
options.misconception_tag: thinks dissolved ions move by osmosis along with water

options.text: Active transport, but no energy is needed because the cell is alive.
options.misconception_tag: thinks active transport happens automatically in living cells without energy cost

stem: Which sub-cellular structure would you expect to find in LARGE numbers in a cell that carries out a lot of active transport?

options.text: Ribosomes, because they release the energy for active transport.
options.misconception_tag: confuses ribosome (protein synthesis) with the site of energy release

options.text: Mitochondria, because they release energy by respiration for active transport.
Chloroplasts, because they make the energy needed for active transport.
options.misconception_tag: thinks chloroplasts supply usable energy for transport / confuses with respiration

options.text: Vacuoles, because they store the energy used in active transport.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the vacuole stores or supplies energy for transport

stem: Glucose in the small intestine is sometimes absorbed by active transport rather than diffusion. In which situation is active transport NEEDED for glucose absorption?

options.text: When the glucose concentration in the gut is higher than in the blood.
options.misconception_tag: thinks active transport is used whenever absorbing glucose, even down a gradient

options.text: When the glucose concentration in the gut is lower than in the blood, so it must move against the gradient.
Whenever glucose is being absorbed, because glucose is too large to diffuse.
options.misconception_tag: thinks glucose is always too large to diffuse and always needs active transport

options.text: Only at night, when the person is not eating and diffusion stops working.
options.misconception_tag: thinks diffusion switches off and active transport is a time-based backup

stem: A student places identical pieces of living plant tissue into mineral ion solutions and measures the uptake of mineral ions. Which change would most reduce the rate of active transport?

options.text: Increasing the concentration of ions in the solution.
options.misconception_tag: assumes higher external concentration always slows uptake, confusing with osmosis/gradient effects

options.text: Lowering the temperature towards 0 degrees C, which slows respiration.
Adding more oxygen to the solution.
options.misconception_tag: thinks oxygen reduces transport, not realising it supports respiration

options.text: Stirring the solution gently to mix the ions.
options.misconception_tag: thinks stirring (mixing) reduces active transport rather than affecting diffusion gradients

stem: Why does active transport STOP if a cell is treated with a poison that blocks aerobic respiration?

options.text: Because the membrane dissolves when respiration stops.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the membrane structure depends directly on respiration

options.text: Because the concentration gradient disappears without respiration.
options.misconception_tag: thinks respiration creates the gradient rather than supplying energy to move against it

options.text: Because active transport needs energy released by respiration, so no respiration means no energy to move ions against the gradient.
Because diffusion takes over and moves ions the other way.
options.misconception_tag: thinks diffusion replaces and reverses active transport when respiration stops

stem: Active transport and diffusion are both ways particles cross membranes. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?

options.text: Active transport needs energy and can go against a gradient; diffusion needs no energy and goes down a gradient.
Active transport needs no energy; diffusion needs energy from respiration.
options.misconception_tag: swaps the energy requirement between the two processes

options.text: Both processes go down a concentration gradient, but active transport is faster.
options.misconception_tag: thinks active transport just means fast diffusion down a gradient

options.text: Active transport only moves water; diffusion only moves dissolved solutes.
options.misconception_tag: confuses active transport with osmosis and restricts diffusion to solutes

stem: The graph of ion uptake against oxygen concentration for living root tissue shows uptake increasing as oxygen rises, then levelling off. What best explains the levelling off at high oxygen?

options.text: Oxygen has become poisonous to the cells, stopping uptake.
options.misconception_tag: thinks excess oxygen poisons cells and halts transport

options.text: Another factor, such as the number of carrier proteins or rate of respiration, has become limiting.
The ions have all been used up inside the cell.
options.misconception_tag: thinks ions are consumed so uptake stops, ignoring limiting factors

options.text: Diffusion has taken over because oxygen is now high.
options.misconception_tag: thinks high oxygen switches the process to diffusion

stem: In active transport, ions are carried across the membrane by carrier (transport) proteins. What is the role of these proteins?

options.text: They make the membrane fully permeable so all particles can pass freely.
options.misconception_tag: thinks carrier proteins make the membrane non-selective

options.text: They release the energy needed for transport by respiring.
options.misconception_tag: thinks carrier proteins themselves carry out respiration to release energy

options.text: They bind specific ions and use energy to move them across the membrane against the gradient.
They pump water across the membrane to dilute the ions.
options.misconception_tag: confuses the carrier protein's role with water movement / osmosis

stem: A potato cell and a similar dead, boiled potato cell are placed in a dilute mineral ion solution. The living cell takes up far more ions. Why does the boiled cell take up almost none by active transport?

options.text: Boiling denatures the carrier proteins and stops respiration, so there is no working transport mechanism or energy.
The boiled cell has a higher ion concentration so it cannot take in more.
options.misconception_tag: explains the result by concentration gradient instead of loss of living function

options.text: Dead cells repel ions because they have no charge.
options.misconception_tag: invents a charge-repulsion idea instead of loss of active mechanism

options.text: Boiling makes the membrane completely waterproof so nothing can enter.
options.misconception_tag: thinks a boiled membrane becomes an impermeable barrier rather than damaged/leaky

stem: Which statement about the energy used in active transport is correct?

options.text: The energy comes directly from sunlight absorbed by the cell.
options.misconception_tag: thinks active transport is directly powered by light, confusing with photosynthesis

options.text: The energy is released during respiration and is used to move particles against their gradient.
No energy is used because the particles move on their own.
options.misconception_tag: thinks active transport is passive and requires no energy

options.text: Energy is only needed to move particles down the concentration gradient.
options.misconception_tag: thinks energy is needed for movement down a gradient rather than against it

stem: A plant is left in waterlogged soil where the spaces between soil particles are filled with water instead of air. Why does the plant struggle to absorb mineral ions from this soil?

options.text: The water washes the mineral ions out of the soil so there are none left.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the problem is loss of ions rather than lack of oxygen for respiration

options.text: The roots cannot get enough oxygen, so respiration falls and there is less energy for active transport of ions.
Too much water enters by osmosis, so ions cannot fit in.
options.misconception_tag: thinks water uptake physically blocks ion uptake

options.text: Active transport speeds up too much and exhausts the roots.
options.misconception_tag: thinks waterlogging increases active transport rather than limiting it

stem: Which combination correctly lists processes that REQUIRE energy from respiration and those that do NOT?

options.text: Requires energy: diffusion and osmosis. Does not: active transport.
options.misconception_tag: reverses which processes need energy

options.text: Requires energy: osmosis only. Does not: diffusion and active transport.
options.misconception_tag: thinks osmosis is the energy-requiring process and active transport is passive

options.text: Requires energy: active transport. Does not: diffusion and osmosis.
All three (diffusion, osmosis and active transport) require energy from respiration.
options.misconception_tag: thinks every form of membrane transport requires respiratory energy

stem: In which stage of the cell cycle does the cell make copies of its DNA (DNA replication) and synthesise the extra sub-cellular structures it needs before dividing?

options.text: During mitosis itself, as the chromosomes line up.
options.misconception_tag: thinks DNA is copied during mitosis rather than beforehand in interphase

options.text: During interphase, before mitosis begins.
During cytokinesis, when the cytoplasm splits.
options.misconception_tag: confuses cell-division stages; thinks DNA copies during cytoplasm division

options.text: Only after the two daughter cells have separated.
options.misconception_tag: thinks DNA replication happens after division, not before

stem: A body cell of an organism contains 16 chromosomes. How many chromosomes will each daughter cell have immediately after this cell divides by mitosis?

options.text: 8, because the chromosome number is halved.
options.misconception_tag: confuses mitosis with meiosis; thinks mitosis halves chromosome number

options.text: 32, because the DNA was doubled during replication.
options.misconception_tag: thinks daughter cells keep the doubled amount instead of it being shared between two cells

options.text: 16, the same as the parent cell.
4, because the chromosomes are divided among four cells.
options.misconception_tag: thinks mitosis produces four daughter cells (confuses with meiosis)

stem: Why is mitosis important in a multicellular organism such as a human?

options.text: It produces gametes (sex cells) for sexual reproduction.
options.misconception_tag: confuses mitosis with meiosis, which produces gametes

options.text: It produces genetically varied cells to help the organism adapt.
options.misconception_tag: thinks mitosis creates variation; it actually produces genetically identical cells

options.text: It produces genetically identical cells for growth and repair of tissues.

options.misconception_tag: thinks mitosis halves chromosome number (confuses with meiosis)

stem: How do the two daughter cells produced by mitosis compare genetically with the parent cell?

options.text: They are genetically identical to each other and to the parent cell.
They are genetically different from each other but identical to the parent.
options.misconception_tag: thinks mitosis introduces variation between daughter cells

options.text: They each have half the genetic information of the parent cell.
options.misconception_tag: confuses mitosis with meiosis; thinks genetic information is halved

options.text: They are identical to each other but different from the parent cell.
options.misconception_tag: thinks daughter cells differ genetically from the parent

stem: During mitosis, what happens to each chromosome (made of two sister chromatids) as the cell divides?

options.text: Each chromosome pairs with a similar chromosome and they swap sections.
options.misconception_tag: confuses mitosis with meiosis (crossing over / pairing of homologous chromosomes)

options.text: The two chromatids of each chromosome are pulled to opposite ends of the cell.
Whole chromosomes line up in pairs and one of each pair goes to each cell.
options.misconception_tag: describes meiosis (separation of homologous pairs) instead of mitosis

options.text: The chromosomes dissolve and are rebuilt in each daughter cell.
options.misconception_tag: thinks chromosomes are destroyed and remade rather than separated

stem: Put these events of the cell cycle in the correct order, from first to last.

options.text: Cell grows and DNA replicates, then mitosis (nucleus divides), then cytoplasm divides.
Mitosis (nucleus divides), then DNA replicates, then cell grows.
options.misconception_tag: thinks DNA is copied after mitosis rather than during interphase before it

options.misconception_tag: thinks the cytoplasm splits before DNA is copied

options.text: DNA replicates, then cytoplasm divides, then mitosis (nucleus divides).
options.misconception_tag: thinks the cytoplasm divides before the nucleus divides

stem: Cancer is best described as the result of which of the following?

options.text: Cells that stop dividing altogether and die off too quickly.
options.misconception_tag: thinks cancer is caused by too little cell division rather than uncontrolled division

options.text: Uncontrolled cell division producing a mass of cells (a tumour).
Cells dividing by meiosis instead of mitosis.
options.misconception_tag: thinks cancer arises from using meiosis instead of mitosis

options.text: Cells that have too few chromosomes after dividing.
options.misconception_tag: thinks cancer is caused by loss of chromosomes during division

stem: Why must a cell copy its DNA before it divides by mitosis?

options.text: So that each daughter cell receives a complete set of genetic information.
So that the daughter cells will be genetically different from each other.
options.misconception_tag: thinks copying DNA creates variation between daughter cells

options.text: So that the chromosome number is doubled in each daughter cell.
options.misconception_tag: thinks daughter cells end up with double the chromosomes

options.text: So that the cell can produce gametes for reproduction.
options.misconception_tag: confuses the purpose of mitosis with gamete production (meiosis)

stem: A scientist counts cells in a sample of tissue and finds that 60% are in interphase and only a small percentage are visibly undergoing mitosis. What does this most likely tell us?

options.text: The tissue is dying because so few cells are dividing.
options.misconception_tag: thinks a low proportion in mitosis means cells are unhealthy/dying

options.text: Most of the cell cycle is spent in interphase, with mitosis taking up a short part of it.
Interphase is not really part of the cell cycle, just a resting gap.
options.misconception_tag: thinks interphase is an inactive 'resting' stage outside the cell cycle

options.misconception_tag: assumes any non-mitosis cells must be in meiosis

stem: Stem cells are useful in medicine and in growth because of which property?

options.text: They have already specialised and so can replace any damaged tissue directly.
options.misconception_tag: thinks stem cells are already specialised rather than undifferentiated

options.text: They divide by meiosis to produce a large variety of new cell types.
options.misconception_tag: thinks stem cells use meiosis and create variation to specialise

options.text: They are undifferentiated and can divide to produce many specialised cell types.
They cannot divide, so they remain unchanged to protect the genome.
options.misconception_tag: thinks stem cells do not divide / are inactive

stem: Before mitosis starts, what happens to the number of sub-cellular structures such as mitochondria and ribosomes in the cell?

options.text: Their number increases so each daughter cell gets enough to function.
Their number stays the same and they are simply shared out unchanged.
options.misconception_tag: thinks only DNA is copied and organelles are merely split, not increased

options.text: They are broken down and only rebuilt after division is complete.
options.misconception_tag: thinks organelles are destroyed before division rather than increased

options.misconception_tag: thinks interphase preparation involves DNA only, not organelle synthesis

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes mitosis from meiosis?

options.text: Mitosis produces two identical cells; meiosis produces four cells with half the chromosome number.
Mitosis produces four genetically different cells; meiosis produces two identical cells.
options.misconception_tag: reverses the cell numbers and variation outcomes of mitosis and meiosis

options.text: Both produce identical cells, but mitosis halves the chromosome number.
options.misconception_tag: thinks mitosis halves chromosome number like meiosis

options.text: Mitosis is only used to make gametes; meiosis is used for growth and repair.
options.misconception_tag: swaps the roles of mitosis (growth/repair) and meiosis (gametes)

stem: A single cell with 46 chromosomes divides by mitosis three times in a row. How many cells, and how many chromosomes per cell, result?

options.text: 8 cells, each with 46 chromosomes.
6 cells, each with 46 chromosomes.

options.misconception_tag: thinks mitosis halves chromosome number each division

options.misconception_tag: thinks each round of division produces only one extra cell

stem: Enzymes are described as biological catalysts. What does this mean for a chemical reaction in a cell?

options.text: The enzyme speeds up the rate of the reaction without being used up itself.
The enzyme is used up during the reaction and must be replaced each time.
options.misconception_tag: thinks enzymes are consumed/used up in the reaction like a reactant

options.text: The enzyme provides the energy needed to make the reaction happen.
options.misconception_tag: thinks enzymes supply energy rather than lowering activation energy

options.text: The enzyme allows a reaction to occur that could never happen without it.
options.misconception_tag: thinks enzymes make impossible reactions possible rather than speeding up existing ones

stem: An enzyme only catalyses one specific reaction. Which feature of the enzyme best explains this specificity?

options.text: Each enzyme has a uniquely shaped active site that fits only one substrate.
Each enzyme can change its shape to fit any substrate it meets.
options.misconception_tag: thinks one enzyme can adapt to bind many different substrates

options.text: Each enzyme works only at one fixed temperature found in the body.
options.misconception_tag: confuses specificity of substrate with temperature optimum

options.text: Each enzyme is made from a different sugar that matches its substrate.
options.misconception_tag: thinks enzymes are carbohydrates rather than proteins

stem: The 'lock and key' model is used to describe enzyme action. In this model, what does the 'key' represent?

options.text: The substrate molecule that fits into the active site.
The active site of the enzyme.
options.misconception_tag: reverses the model: thinks the active site (lock) is the key

options.text: The product released after the reaction.
options.misconception_tag: confuses the substrate that enters with the product that leaves

options.text: The whole enzyme molecule.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the key represents the entire enzyme rather than the substrate

stem: As temperature rises from 10 °C to 37 °C, the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction in the human body increases. Which statement best explains this increase?

options.text: The enzyme and substrate molecules have more kinetic energy, so they collide more often and successfully.

options.misconception_tag: thinks heat increases rate by enlarging the enzyme rather than increasing collisions

options.text: The higher temperature changes the shape of the active site so it fits the substrate better.
options.misconception_tag: thinks heating below the optimum improves active-site fit

options.text: The higher temperature makes more enzyme molecules form inside the cell.
options.misconception_tag: thinks raising temperature creates more enzyme molecules

stem: A student heats an enzyme to 70 °C and finds it no longer works, even after cooling it back to 37 °C. What has happened to the enzyme?

options.text: The active site has changed shape permanently, so the substrate no longer fits — it has denatured.
The enzyme has been killed and is now dead.
options.misconception_tag: thinks enzymes are alive and can be 'killed'

options.text: The enzyme has been used up by the high temperature.
options.misconception_tag: thinks high temperature consumes the enzyme rather than denaturing it

options.text: The enzyme has melted but will work again once it is cool.
options.misconception_tag: thinks denaturing is reversible on cooling

stem: The enzyme pepsin works in the stomach at about pH 2, while amylase in the mouth works best at about pH 7. Why does pepsin NOT work well in the mouth?

All enzymes in the body work best at exactly pH 7.
options.misconception_tag: thinks every enzyme has the same neutral pH optimum

options.text: The mouth is too cold for pepsin to be active.
options.misconception_tag: attributes a pH effect to temperature instead

options.text: There is no substrate for pepsin anywhere in the body except the stomach.
options.misconception_tag: confuses location of optimum pH with availability of substrate

stem: Two test tubes contain the same starch solution and amylase. Tube A is at pH 6 and Tube B is at pH 9, both at 37 °C. Amylase has an optimum of pH 7. In which tube will starch be broken down faster, and why?

options.text: Tube A, because pH 6 is closer to the enzyme's optimum pH than pH 9.
Tube B, because a higher pH always means a faster reaction.

Substrate: glucose → Product: starch.

stem: Lipase is an enzyme that breaks down a large food molecule. Which statement correctly describes the substrate and products of lipase?

options.text: It breaks down proteins into amino acids.
options.misconception_tag: confuses lipase with protease

stem: When the substrate binds to the active site, a reaction takes place and the products are released. What happens to the enzyme's active site immediately after the products leave?

options.misconception_tag: thinks the active site is changed by binding the product

options.misconception_tag: thinks the active site is incorporated into the product

stem: A graph shows enzyme activity peaking sharply at 40 °C and then falling steeply to zero by 60 °C. Which statement best explains the shape of the curve after the peak?

options.text: Above the optimum, increasing heat denatures the enzyme, changing the active site so the substrate no longer fits, and activity falls.
Above the optimum, the reaction simply runs out of substrate, so activity falls.

options.text: Above the optimum, the molecules move so fast they bounce off each other and never collide.
options.misconception_tag: thinks faster molecules collide less, not denaturing

options.misconception_tag: denies any real fall in enzyme activity above the optimum

stem: Bile is produced by the liver and released into the small intestine. Bile is NOT an enzyme, but it helps lipase digest fats. How does bile increase the rate of fat digestion?

stem: Which row correctly matches a digestive enzyme to the food group it breaks down?

options.misconception_tag: confuses the substrate and products of lipase

stem: What are the final products when a protein is fully digested?

options.misconception_tag: confuses protein products with lipid products

stem: Lipase digests lipids (fats). What are the products of this reaction?

Glucose and glycogen.

options.text: Amino acids.
options.misconception_tag: confuses lipid products with protein products

options.text: Simple sugars and glycerol.

stem: Bile is alkaline. Why is it important that bile is added to food as it leaves the stomach and enters the small intestine?

stem: Where is amylase produced in the digestive system?

Only in the stomach.

stem: Why must large starch and protein molecules be digested into smaller molecules before the body can use them?

stem: An enzyme is described as a biological catalyst. What does this mean for digestion?

stem: A student investigates how pH affects amylase. At pH 2 the amylase no longer breaks down any starch, even after a long time. What is the best explanation?

stem: In the 'lock and key' model, why does a particular enzyme only digest one type of food molecule?

stem: A digestion experiment using a Benedict's test is run at 0°C, 30°C and 60°C to see how temperature affects amylase. Why might amylase break down very little starch at BOTH 0°C and 60°C?

stem: In the human double circulatory system, how many times does the blood pass through the heart for one complete circuit of the body?
