options.text: Deoxygenated blood on its way to the lungs.
options.misconception_tag: confuses the pulmonary vein with the pulmonary artery

stem: The natural resting heart rate is controlled by a group of cells that act as a pacemaker. Where are these cells found?

options.text: In the wall of the right atrium.
In the wall of the left ventricle.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the pacemaker is in the strongest pumping chamber, the left ventricle

options.text: In the brain, which sends the timing signals to the heart.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the heartbeat is generated by the brain rather than by pacemaker cells in the heart itself

options.text: In the aorta, where blood leaves the heart.
options.misconception_tag: confuses the location of the pacemaker with a major blood vessel

stem: A patient has a faulty natural pacemaker, causing an irregular heartbeat. Which device is normally used to correct this?

options.text: An artificial pacemaker.
A stent.
options.misconception_tag: confuses a pacemaker with a stent, which widens narrowed coronary arteries

options.text: A statin.
options.misconception_tag: thinks a drug that lowers cholesterol can correct an electrical timing problem

options.text: A mechanical heart valve.
options.misconception_tag: confuses an electrical rhythm problem with a faulty valve

stem: The heart muscle itself needs its own supply of oxygenated blood. Which vessels provide this?

options.text: The coronary arteries.
The pulmonary arteries.
options.misconception_tag: confuses the coronary arteries supplying the heart muscle with the pulmonary arteries to the lungs

options.text: The blood already passing through the heart's chambers supplies the muscle directly.
options.misconception_tag: thinks blood in the chambers diffuses into and feeds the heart wall, so no separate supply is needed

options.text: The vena cava.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the heart muscle is supplied by the large vein returning blood to the heart

stem: In coronary heart disease, fatty material builds up in the coronary arteries. Why is this dangerous?

options.text: Less oxygenated blood reaches the heart muscle, so it cannot respire enough to keep contracting.
The blood inside the heart's chambers becomes blocked and cannot be pumped out.
options.misconception_tag: thinks coronary arteries carry the blood being pumped through the heart, not the blood supplying the muscle

options.text: Oxygen can no longer pass from the lungs into the blood.
options.misconception_tag: confuses a coronary artery blockage with a gas-exchange problem in the lungs

options.text: The heart muscle receives too much oxygen and works too hard.
options.misconception_tag: thinks narrowing the artery increases oxygen delivery rather than reducing it

stem: Which sequence correctly traces blood through the LEFT side of the heart?

options.text: Pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta.
Vena cava → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the vena cava empties into the left atrium; it actually returns to the right atrium

options.text: Pulmonary artery → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta.
options.misconception_tag: confuses the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein when feeding the left atrium

options.text: Pulmonary vein → left ventricle → left atrium → aorta.
options.misconception_tag: reverses the order of atrium and ventricle in the path through the heart

stem: A blood vessel is described as carrying deoxygenated blood AWAY from the heart at high pressure. Which vessel is it?

options.text: The pulmonary artery.
The pulmonary vein.
options.misconception_tag: thinks any vessel carrying deoxygenated blood must be a vein

options.text: The vena cava.
options.misconception_tag: associates 'deoxygenated' only with the vena cava, ignoring 'away from the heart'

options.text: The aorta.
options.misconception_tag: assumes a high-pressure artery leaving the heart must carry oxygenated blood

stem: Why does the heart need a septum, the solid wall of muscle running down its middle?

options.text: To keep oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from mixing inside the heart.
To stop blood flowing backwards between the atria and ventricles.
options.misconception_tag: confuses the role of the septum with the role of the heart valves

options.text: To act as the pacemaker that sets the heart rate.
options.misconception_tag: confuses the structural dividing wall with the electrical pacemaker tissue

options.text: To pump the blood out of the heart into the arteries.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the septum actively pumps rather than being a dividing wall

stem: An artery and a vein are viewed under a microscope. Which feature is used to identify the vessel as an ARTERY rather than a vein?

options.text: It has a thick muscular and elastic wall with a relatively small lumen.
It has a large lumen and a thin wall containing valves.
options.misconception_tag: swaps the structural features of arteries and veins

options.text: It is the only vessel with a wall just one cell thick.
options.misconception_tag: confuses arteries with capillaries

options.text: It always carries blood that is bright red because it is oxygenated.
options.misconception_tag: identifies arteries by blood colour and ignores pulmonary artery exception

stem: Why do veins contain valves, but arteries do not?

options.text: Blood in veins is at low pressure, so valves are needed to stop it flowing backwards.
Veins carry deoxygenated blood, and valves are needed to filter out the carbon dioxide.
options.misconception_tag: thinks valves remove or filter substances from the blood

options.text: Blood in veins moves too fast, so valves slow it down before it reaches the heart.
options.misconception_tag: thinks venous blood is fast and valves act as a brake

options.text: Veins carry blood away from the heart, so valves are needed to push it outwards.
options.misconception_tag: thinks veins carry blood away from the heart

stem: Which statement correctly describes the direction of blood flow in arteries and veins?

options.text: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry blood towards the heart.
Arteries carry blood towards the heart and veins carry blood away from the heart.
options.misconception_tag: reverses the direction of flow in arteries and veins

options.text: Arteries always carry oxygenated blood and veins always carry deoxygenated blood.
options.misconception_tag: defines arteries/veins by oxygenation rather than direction of flow

options.text: Both arteries and veins carry blood away from the heart to the body cells.
options.misconception_tag: thinks both vessel types carry blood away from the heart

stem: A capillary wall is only one cell thick. How does this feature help the capillary carry out its function?

options.text: It gives a short diffusion distance, so substances are exchanged quickly between blood and cells.
It allows the capillary to stretch and recoil to keep the blood at high pressure.
options.misconception_tag: attributes the elastic-recoil function of arteries to capillaries

options.text: It lets whole red blood cells leak out of the capillary into the tissues.
options.misconception_tag: thinks red blood cells routinely pass through the capillary wall

options.text: It allows the capillary to actively pump glucose into the cells using energy.
options.misconception_tag: thinks exchange across the capillary wall is active transport, not diffusion

stem: Which blood vessel is the EXCEPTION to the general rule that arteries carry oxygenated blood?

options.text: The pulmonary artery, which carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
The pulmonary vein, which carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
options.misconception_tag: confuses the pulmonary vein with the pulmonary artery

options.text: The aorta, which carries deoxygenated blood from the body.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the aorta carries deoxygenated blood

options.text: There is no exception; every artery in the body carries oxygenated blood.
options.misconception_tag: believes all arteries without exception carry oxygenated blood

stem: The wall of an artery contains thick layers of elastic fibres and muscle. Why is this important for its function?

options.text: It lets the wall stretch and recoil to withstand and smooth out the high pressure of blood from the heart.
It allows the artery to contract and physically pump the blood forward like the heart.
options.misconception_tag: thinks artery walls pump blood rather than withstanding pressure

options.text: It makes the wall thick enough to stop any oxygen diffusing out of the blood.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the thick wall functions to prevent gas exchange

options.text: It provides valves along the artery to keep the blood flowing one way.
options.misconception_tag: thinks arteries contain valves like veins

stem: A student says: 'Capillaries are not very useful because they are so small and thin.' Which response best corrects this idea?

options.text: Capillaries form huge networks that bring blood close to every cell so substances can be exchanged.
Capillaries are only used to store extra blood until the body needs it.
options.misconception_tag: thinks capillaries are blood-storage vessels

options.text: Capillaries are where the blood is first pumped out of the heart at high pressure.
options.misconception_tag: thinks capillaries receive blood directly from the heart at high pressure

options.text: Capillaries carry blood back to the heart against gravity using valves.
options.misconception_tag: confuses capillary function with the role of veins

stem: In which blood vessel is the blood at the HIGHEST pressure?

options.text: In the arteries, because they receive blood directly from the contracting heart.
In the veins, because their walls are thin and cannot resist the blood.
options.misconception_tag: thinks thin-walled veins carry the highest-pressure blood

options.text: In the capillaries, because their lumen is so narrow that it squeezes the blood.
options.misconception_tag: assumes a narrow lumen automatically means the highest pressure

options.text: The pressure is exactly the same in all blood vessels because it is one connected system.
options.misconception_tag: thinks blood pressure is constant throughout the circulation

stem: Why do veins have a larger lumen than arteries of a similar size?

options.text: A wide lumen reduces resistance, helping low-pressure blood return to the heart more easily.
A wide lumen is needed because veins carry far more blood than arteries.
options.misconception_tag: thinks veins carry a greater volume/amount of blood than arteries

options.text: A wide lumen allows the high-pressure blood from the heart to spread out.
options.misconception_tag: thinks veins carry high-pressure blood from the heart

options.text: A wide lumen is needed so that gas exchange can happen across the vein wall.
options.misconception_tag: thinks gas exchange takes place in veins rather than capillaries

stem: Blood flows through the vessels of the circulatory system in which correct order?

options.text: Artery -> arteriole -> capillary -> venule -> vein.
Vein -> capillary -> artery, going from the heart to the body.
options.misconception_tag: reverses the artery/vein roles in the order of flow

options.text: Artery -> vein -> capillary, with the capillary last before returning to the heart.
options.misconception_tag: places capillaries after veins instead of between artery and vein

options.text: Capillary -> artery -> vein, starting with the smallest vessel at the heart.
options.misconception_tag: thinks blood leaves the heart through capillaries first

stem: The wall of a capillary is described as 'permeable'. What does this allow?

options.text: Dissolved substances such as glucose and oxygen can pass through the wall to the cells.
Large numbers of red blood cells can freely pass out into the tissue fluid.
options.misconception_tag: thinks permeable means red blood cells leave the capillary normally

options.text: Blood can flow backwards through the wall when the pressure drops.
options.misconception_tag: confuses a permeable wall with backflow control by valves

options.text: The capillary can absorb water from the air outside the body.
options.misconception_tag: misunderstands permeability as exchange with the external environment

stem: During exercise, blood vessels supplying the leg muscles widen (vasodilation). What is the main effect of this?

options.text: More blood, carrying oxygen and glucose, can flow to the working muscles.
Less blood reaches the muscles, so they can rest and recover.
options.misconception_tag: thinks widening a vessel reduces the blood flow through it

options.text: The blood becomes more oxygenated as it passes through the wider vessel.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the vessel itself adds oxygen to the blood

options.text: The muscle cells are pumped directly into the bloodstream for energy.
options.misconception_tag: confuses delivery of glucose with movement of whole cells into the blood

stem: Which row correctly matches each vessel to a key structural feature?

options.text: Capillary: one-cell-thick wall; Artery: thick muscular wall; Vein: valves.
Capillary: valves; Artery: one-cell-thick wall; Vein: thick muscular wall.
options.misconception_tag: misassigns the defining feature of each vessel type

options.text: Capillary: thick muscular wall; Artery: valves; Vein: one-cell-thick wall.
options.misconception_tag: completely scrambles structure with function across all three vessels

options.text: Capillary: large lumen; Artery: valves; Vein: one-cell-thick wall.
options.misconception_tag: gives the capillary a large lumen and gives arteries valves

stem: Which word equation correctly summarises photosynthesis?

options.text: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
options.misconception_tag: confuses photosynthesis with aerobic respiration (reverses the equation)

options.text: Carbon dioxide + oxygen → glucose + water
options.misconception_tag: thinks oxygen is a raw material rather than a product

options.text: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + carbon dioxide
options.misconception_tag: does not realise oxygen is the gas produced; recycles a reactant as product

stem: Photosynthesis is described as an endothermic reaction. What does this tell you about energy?

options.text: Energy is transferred from the environment (light) to the plant during the reaction.
Energy is released by the plant into the surroundings as the reaction happens.
options.misconception_tag: confuses endothermic with exothermic (thinks energy is given out)

options.text: No energy is involved because plants make their own food.
options.misconception_tag: thinks 'making your own food' means no external energy is needed

options.text: Energy is created by the chlorophyll inside the chloroplasts.
options.misconception_tag: thinks energy is created rather than transferred/transformed

stem: A plant is kept in conditions of constant temperature and plenty of light, but the amount of carbon dioxide is steadily increased. The rate of photosynthesis rises and then levels off. What is the best explanation for why it levels off?

options.text: Another factor, such as light intensity or temperature, has become the limiting factor.
The plant has run out of carbon dioxide to use.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the factor being increased becomes used up, rather than a different factor limiting

options.text: The plant has made all the glucose it will ever need.
options.misconception_tag: thinks photosynthesis stops once 'enough' glucose is made

options.text: Increasing carbon dioxide always slows photosynthesis down at high levels.
options.misconception_tag: believes raising a factor beyond a point is directly harmful rather than simply no longer limiting

stem: Why does the rate of photosynthesis usually fall if the temperature rises above about 45 °C?

options.text: The enzymes controlling photosynthesis denature, so their active sites change shape.
The enzymes are killed by the high temperature.
options.misconception_tag: describes enzymes as alive and able to be 'killed'

options.text: The carbon dioxide evaporates away before it can be used.
options.misconception_tag: misattributes the temperature effect to loss of a reactant

options.text: The light energy becomes too strong for the chlorophyll to absorb.
options.misconception_tag: confuses a temperature effect with a light-intensity effect

stem: In an experiment, the number of oxygen bubbles released by pondweed is counted at different distances from a lamp. As the lamp is moved further away, fewer bubbles are produced each minute. Why?

options.text: Moving the lamp away decreases the light intensity reaching the pondweed, slowing photosynthesis.
Moving the lamp away cools the water, and the cold stops the bubbles forming.
options.misconception_tag: attributes the change to temperature rather than the controlled light-intensity variable

options.text: The oxygen bubbles get trapped and cannot escape over the longer distance.
options.misconception_tag: invents a physical barrier rather than linking to reduced photosynthesis rate

options.text: Further away there is less carbon dioxide dissolved in the water.
options.misconception_tag: changes the wrong variable; distance from lamp affects light, not CO2

stem: Why is chlorophyll essential for photosynthesis?

options.text: It absorbs light energy, which is then used to drive the reaction.
It releases the oxygen produced during the reaction.
options.misconception_tag: assigns the gas-release role to chlorophyll

options.text: It provides the carbon dioxide needed to make glucose.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the green pigment supplies a raw material

options.text: It makes the leaf green so it can attract more sunlight to it.
options.misconception_tag: thinks colour itself 'attracts' light rather than chlorophyll absorbing it

stem: A leaf that has been kept in the dark for 48 hours tests negative for starch with iodine solution. What does this best show?

options.text: Without light the leaf cannot photosynthesise, so no glucose was made and stored as starch.
The starch already in the leaf was destroyed directly by the darkness.
options.misconception_tag: thinks darkness actively breaks starch down rather than preventing its production

options.text: Light is needed to turn the iodine blue-black, not to make starch.
options.misconception_tag: confuses the role of light in photosynthesis with the chemistry of the iodine test

options.text: The leaf used up all its starch in respiration because it had no oxygen.
options.misconception_tag: introduces an oxygen/respiration explanation not supported by destarching logic

stem: Some of the glucose made in photosynthesis is converted into insoluble starch for storage. Why is starch a more suitable storage molecule than glucose?

options.text: Starch is insoluble, so it does not affect the water moving into or out of the cell by osmosis.
Starch contains more energy per gram than glucose does.
options.misconception_tag: thinks storage form has higher energy density rather than better storage properties

options.text: Starch can be used directly in respiration but glucose cannot.
options.misconception_tag: reverses which molecule is the respiratory substrate

options.text: Starch dissolves easily so it can be transported quickly around the plant.
options.misconception_tag: believes starch is soluble/transportable; confuses it with sugars/sucrose

stem: A market gardener burns a paraffin heater inside a greenhouse on a cold, dark winter evening. Apart from raising the temperature, why might this increase crop yield?

options.text: Burning paraffin releases carbon dioxide, increasing the supply of a raw material for photosynthesis.
Burning paraffin releases extra oxygen that the plants need to photosynthesise.
options.misconception_tag: thinks oxygen is a raw material for photosynthesis

options.text: The flame provides the light energy the plants need overnight.
options.misconception_tag: overstates a heater flame as a meaningful light source for photosynthesis

options.text: The smoke fertilises the soil so the roots can absorb more glucose.
options.misconception_tag: thinks plants absorb glucose from soil rather than making it themselves

stem: Two identical pond plants are given the same light and temperature. Plant X is in water with extra dissolved carbon dioxide; Plant Y is in ordinary water. Plant X photosynthesises faster. In this experiment, what is carbon dioxide acting as?

options.text: The limiting factor for Plant Y, because increasing it speeds the reaction up.
The limiting factor for Plant X, because it has the most carbon dioxide.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the plant with more of a factor is the one being limited by it

options.text: A catalyst that speeds the reaction up without being used.
options.misconception_tag: confuses a reactant/raw material with a catalyst

options.text: A waste product that builds up and is removed faster in Plant X.
options.misconception_tag: classifies CO2 as a product of photosynthesis rather than a reactant

stem: Glucose made by a plant is used in several ways. Which of these is a correct use of that glucose?

options.text: It is used in respiration to release energy for the plant's cells.
It is broken down to release the oxygen the plant breathes in.
options.misconception_tag: thinks glucose is broken down to supply oxygen; confuses gas exchange roles

options.text: It is absorbed by the roots and passed back into the soil.
options.misconception_tag: reverses the direction of glucose movement; thinks plants excrete glucose to soil

options.text: It is converted into chlorophyll to make new green leaves.
options.misconception_tag: thinks glucose is turned directly into the pigment chlorophyll

stem: During the daytime a healthy leaf carries out both photosynthesis and respiration. Which statement about the gases is correct on a bright day?

options.text: The leaf makes more oxygen by photosynthesis than it uses in respiration, so there is a net release of oxygen.
The leaf only photosynthesises in the day and does not respire until night.
options.misconception_tag: thinks respiration switches off during the day / only happens at night

options.text: Photosynthesis and respiration always exactly cancel out, so no gases are exchanged with the air.
options.misconception_tag: assumes the two processes are always balanced regardless of light

options.text: The leaf takes in oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide overall in bright light.
options.misconception_tag: applies the night-time/respiration-only gas pattern to bright daylight

stem: In a photosynthesis experiment, why is it important to keep all variables constant except the one being investigated?

options.text: So that any change in the rate can be confidently linked to the one factor being changed.
So that the plant can photosynthesise as fast as it possibly can.
options.misconception_tag: thinks control variables are about maximising the rate rather than fair testing

options.text: Because changing more than one factor would damage the plant.
options.misconception_tag: believes the reason is plant safety rather than experimental validity

options.text: So the experiment finishes more quickly and gives a result sooner.
options.misconception_tag: confuses the purpose of controls with speeding up the procedure

stem: A plant is photosynthesising in a brightly lit room at 20 C. The rate of photosynthesis is currently limited by carbon dioxide concentration. What single change would increase the rate the MOST?

options.text: Increasing the carbon dioxide concentration around the plant.
Increasing the light intensity by moving the lamp closer.
options.misconception_tag: thinks adding more of any factor speeds up photosynthesis, ignoring which factor is actually limiting

options.text: Increasing the temperature towards 40 C.
options.misconception_tag: assumes raising temperature always increases rate and ignores the identified limiting factor

options.text: Giving the plant more water through its roots.
options.misconception_tag: treats water as a limiting factor of photosynthesis rate in normal conditions

stem: On a graph of rate of photosynthesis against light intensity, the line rises steeply and then flattens into a horizontal plateau. What does the plateau region tell us?

options.text: Something other than light (e.g. CO2 or temperature) is now limiting the rate.
Light intensity has stopped increasing, so the rate cannot rise.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the x-axis variable has stopped changing rather than realising another factor limits the rate

options.text: The plant has run out of chlorophyll and can no longer absorb light.
options.misconception_tag: invents chlorophyll depletion instead of identifying a different limiting factor

options.text: Photosynthesis has stopped completely at this point.
options.misconception_tag: confuses a constant (plateaued) rate with a rate of zero

stem: The rate of photosynthesis increases as temperature rises from 5 C to about 40 C, then falls sharply at higher temperatures. What is the BEST explanation for the sharp fall above 40 C?

options.text: Enzymes controlling photosynthesis are denatured, so their active sites change shape.
The enzymes are killed by the high temperature.
options.misconception_tag: describes enzymes as alive and able to be 'killed' rather than denatured

options.text: Carbon dioxide is used up faster than it can be replaced.
options.misconception_tag: attributes the high-temperature fall to CO2 shortage rather than enzyme denaturation

options.text: The light reaction speeds up so much that the plant overheats and stops.
options.misconception_tag: gives a vague 'overheating' idea instead of the denaturation of enzymes

stem: A grower wants to maximise photosynthesis in a greenhouse on a warm, sunny summer day. Which factor is MOST likely to be the limiting factor that they should increase?

options.text: Carbon dioxide concentration.
Light intensity.
options.misconception_tag: assumes light is limiting even when sunlight is already plentiful

options.text: Temperature.
options.misconception_tag: assumes temperature is limiting on an already warm day

options.text: Water supply to the roots.
options.misconception_tag: treats water as the controllable limiting factor of photosynthesis rate

stem: Two identical plants are kept at the same light intensity and same CO2 level. Plant X is at 15 C and Plant Y is at 30 C. Plant Y photosynthesises faster. Which is the BEST explanation, assuming no enzymes are denatured?

options.text: Higher temperature gives molecules more kinetic energy and increases enzyme activity, speeding up the reactions.
Higher temperature provides extra energy that replaces the need for light.
options.misconception_tag: thinks heat can substitute for light energy in photosynthesis

options.text: Higher temperature directly produces more carbon dioxide for the plant to use.
options.misconception_tag: thinks warmth creates additional CO2 supply rather than speeding enzyme-controlled reactions

options.text: Warmth opens the stomata wider so more glucose enters the leaf.
options.misconception_tag: thinks glucose enters the leaf from outside rather than being made inside it

stem: At night, a sealed greenhouse has no light. Which factor is limiting the rate of photosynthesis, and what is happening to the plant?

options.text: Light is the limiting factor; photosynthesis is not occurring, though the plant still respires.
Carbon dioxide is the limiting factor; the plant continues to photosynthesise slowly.
options.misconception_tag: thinks photosynthesis continues in the dark, just more slowly

options.text: Temperature is the limiting factor; the plant stops both photosynthesis and respiration.
options.misconception_tag: thinks respiration stops when photosynthesis stops

options.text: No factor is limiting because the plant switches to using oxygen to make glucose at night.
options.misconception_tag: believes the plant makes glucose at night by reversing the process

stem: A graph shows rate of photosynthesis against CO2 concentration at two light intensities: a higher curve for bright light and a lower curve for dim light. Both curves eventually level off. Why does the bright-light curve level off at a HIGHER rate?

options.text: At high CO2 the rate is limited by light, and brighter light allows a higher maximum rate before levelling off.
Bright light produces more carbon dioxide, so its curve is always higher.
options.misconception_tag: thinks increasing light increases the CO2 supply

options.text: The two curves level off at the same point because CO2 is the only factor shown.
options.misconception_tag: ignores that light limits the maximum rate once CO2 is plentiful

options.text: Bright light raises the temperature, and temperature is the only factor that sets the maximum rate.
options.misconception_tag: attributes the higher plateau solely to temperature rather than to light as the limiting factor

stem: A student claims: 'If I keep increasing the light intensity, the rate of photosynthesis will keep increasing forever.' Why is this claim INCORRECT?

options.text: Eventually another factor, such as CO2 or temperature, becomes limiting and the rate stops rising.
Very bright light always denatures the plant's enzymes, so the rate falls to zero.
options.misconception_tag: thinks light intensity itself denatures enzymes like high temperature does

options.text: Light intensity has no effect on the rate of photosynthesis at all.
options.misconception_tag: overcorrects and denies that light affects rate

options.text: The plant can only absorb a fixed total amount of light each day regardless of intensity.
options.misconception_tag: invents a daily light 'quota' rather than identifying another limiting factor

stem: Commercial greenhouse growers sometimes burn fuels such as paraffin inside the greenhouse. Which TWO limiting factors does this practice increase, helping photosynthesis?

options.text: Carbon dioxide concentration and temperature.
Light intensity and temperature.
options.misconception_tag: thinks burning fuel mainly provides extra light for the plants

options.text: Oxygen concentration and water.
options.misconception_tag: thinks supplying oxygen increases the rate of photosynthesis

options.text: Carbon dioxide concentration and light intensity.
options.misconception_tag: correctly identifies CO2 but wrongly adds light rather than the warmth produced by burning the fuel

stem: The rate of a reaction limited by CO2 is being measured. Which statement correctly describes what 'CO2 is the limiting factor' actually means?

options.text: CO2 is in shortest supply relative to need, so increasing it would increase the rate while the other factors stay the same.
CO2 is the only factor that affects the rate of photosynthesis.
options.misconception_tag: thinks a limiting factor is the only factor that ever matters

options.text: There is no CO2 left, so photosynthesis has completely stopped.
options.misconception_tag: confuses 'limiting' with 'completely absent'

options.text: CO2 has reached its maximum useful level and adding more would slow the rate.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the limiting factor is the one already in excess

stem: A greenhouse is kept at the ideal CO2 level and ideal light intensity, but the temperature is only 5 C. The rate of photosynthesis is low. What is the BEST way to increase it?

options.text: Warm the greenhouse towards the optimum temperature for the plant's enzymes.
Add even more carbon dioxide than the ideal level.
options.misconception_tag: tries to increase a factor that is already at its ideal level

options.text: Increase the light intensity further still.
options.misconception_tag: increases a non-limiting factor instead of the limiting one (temperature)

options.text: Cool the greenhouse further to protect the enzymes from denaturing.
options.misconception_tag: thinks lowering temperature protects enzymes and helps a slow reaction

stem: Why can artificially raising the carbon dioxide level in a greenhouse to about 0.1% increase crop yield, even though normal air contains only about 0.04% CO2?

options.text: At normal levels CO2 limits the rate, so adding more removes that limit and allows faster photosynthesis.
Extra CO2 is needed because plants respire the same gas they use for photosynthesis.
options.misconception_tag: muddles the gases of respiration and photosynthesis

options.text: Extra CO2 increases the light intensity inside the greenhouse.
options.misconception_tag: thinks CO2 affects light levels

options.text: Extra CO2 makes the plant grow because CO2 is the plant's main food.
options.misconception_tag: treats CO2 itself as 'food' rather than a raw material made into glucose

stem: A pondweed setup measures oxygen bubbles per minute as a proxy for photosynthesis rate. The lamp is kept very close, but a heat shield (a flask of water) is placed between the lamp and the pondweed. Why is the heat shield used?

options.text: To absorb heat so that temperature stays constant and only light intensity is the variable being tested.
To increase the light intensity reaching the pondweed by focusing the beam.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the water flask acts as a lens to boost light rather than control temperature

options.text: To supply extra carbon dioxide dissolved in the water to the pondweed.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the heat shield provides CO2 to the plant

options.text: To reduce the light intensity so the pondweed is not damaged.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the shield is there to dim the light rather than block heat

stem: Which word equation correctly represents aerobic respiration?

options.text: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
glucose + carbon dioxide → oxygen + water
options.misconception_tag: confuses respiration with photosynthesis (reverses reactants and products)

options.text: glucose → lactic acid
options.misconception_tag: confuses aerobic respiration with anaerobic respiration in muscle

options.text: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
options.misconception_tag: writes the photosynthesis equation instead of respiration

stem: In which part of the cell does aerobic respiration mainly take place?

options.text: The chloroplast
options.misconception_tag: confuses the site of respiration with the site of photosynthesis

options.text: The nucleus
options.misconception_tag: assumes all key cell reactions happen in the nucleus

options.text: The mitochondria
The ribosomes
options.misconception_tag: confuses respiration with the site of protein synthesis

stem: A student says respiration is an exothermic reaction. Which statement BEST justifies this?

options.text: It transfers energy to the surroundings, which is why exercising organisms warm up
It takes in energy from the surroundings, which is why it needs oxygen
options.misconception_tag: thinks respiration is endothermic / absorbs energy

options.text: It transfers energy because it produces light, like a glow stick
options.misconception_tag: thinks exothermic reactions must release light energy

options.text: It is exothermic only when it happens without oxygen
options.misconception_tag: confuses exothermic respiration with anaerobic conditions

stem: Why do cells need a continuous supply of energy from respiration, even when an organism is resting?

options.text: Because energy is needed for processes such as building larger molecules, active transport and keeping warm
Because energy is only needed to move muscles, and resting muscles still twitch
options.misconception_tag: thinks respiration energy is only for movement

options.text: Because the cell must keep making oxygen to stay alive
options.misconception_tag: thinks respiration produces oxygen the cell needs

options.text: Because glucose must be broken down to stop it building up and poisoning the cell
options.misconception_tag: thinks the purpose of respiration is to remove excess glucose rather than release energy

stem: Compared with anaerobic respiration, why does aerobic respiration transfer much more energy per glucose molecule?

options.text: Because glucose is completely broken down to carbon dioxide and water when oxygen is present
Because aerobic respiration happens faster than anaerobic respiration
options.misconception_tag: confuses rate of reaction with amount of energy transferred

options.text: Because aerobic respiration produces lactic acid, which stores extra energy
options.misconception_tag: thinks aerobic respiration produces lactic acid

options.text: Because aerobic respiration does not need glucose, only oxygen
options.misconception_tag: thinks oxygen rather than glucose is the energy source

stem: The rate of aerobic respiration in an organism can be estimated by measuring which of the following?

options.text: The rate at which carbon dioxide is produced or oxygen is used up
The rate at which oxygen is produced
options.misconception_tag: thinks respiration releases oxygen rather than using it

options.text: The rate at which glucose is made by the cell
options.misconception_tag: thinks respiration synthesises glucose

options.text: The rate at which water is taken into the cell
options.misconception_tag: confuses water as a reactant taken in rather than a product

stem: During hard exercise, a person's breathing rate and heart rate both increase. What is the main reason for this?

options.text: To deliver more oxygen and glucose to muscles and remove the extra carbon dioxide produced by faster respiration
To deliver more carbon dioxide to the muscles so they can respire faster
options.misconception_tag: thinks carbon dioxide is a reactant supplied to muscles

options.text: To cool the body down by moving air in and out more quickly
options.misconception_tag: thinks faster breathing is only about cooling, not gas exchange for respiration

options.text: To remove the extra oxygen made by the muscles during exercise
options.misconception_tag: thinks respiring muscles produce oxygen

stem: Why is aerobic respiration described as a series of enzyme-controlled reactions rather than a single reaction?

options.text: Energy is released gradually in small steps, each controlled by a different enzyme, so it is not lost all at once
One enzyme breaks the whole glucose molecule apart in a single fast step
options.misconception_tag: thinks respiration is one big reaction rather than many small steps

options.text: Enzymes are used up in the reaction, so many are needed to keep it going
options.misconception_tag: thinks enzymes are used up / are reactants

options.text: The reactions must happen slowly because enzymes slow chemical reactions down
options.misconception_tag: thinks enzymes slow reactions rather than act as catalysts

stem: A respirometer shows woodlice using oxygen faster at 25°C than at 5°C. What is the best explanation?

options.text: At a higher temperature the enzymes controlling respiration work faster, so the rate of respiration increases
At a higher temperature the woodlice need less oxygen, so they breathe faster to get rid of it
options.misconception_tag: confuses using oxygen with getting rid of oxygen

options.text: Higher temperatures denature the enzymes, which speeds up respiration
options.misconception_tag: thinks denaturing enzymes increases reaction rate

options.text: At a higher temperature the woodlice photosynthesise faster, using more oxygen
options.misconception_tag: thinks animals photosynthesise / confuses respiration with photosynthesis

stem: Both photosynthesis and aerobic respiration occur in a leaf cell. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Respiration happens in the cell all the time, while photosynthesis only happens when there is enough light
Photosynthesis happens all the time, while respiration only happens at night
options.misconception_tag: thinks respiration only occurs in the dark / at night

options.text: Respiration stops during the day because photosynthesis takes over
options.misconception_tag: thinks the two processes cannot occur at the same time

options.text: Both processes only happen during the day when the plant is active
options.misconception_tag: thinks respiration only happens when the plant is in the light

stem: Why does the amount of energy actually available to do useful work in a cell turn out to be less than the total chemical energy stored in glucose?

options.text: Some of the energy is transferred to the surroundings as heat during respiration
Some of the glucose is destroyed and its energy disappears completely
options.misconception_tag: thinks energy is destroyed, violating conservation of energy

options.text: Some energy is used up making oxygen for the next reaction
options.misconception_tag: thinks oxygen is produced and energy is spent making it

options.text: Some energy is converted back into new glucose by the mitochondria
options.misconception_tag: thinks mitochondria rebuild glucose

stem: Where do the carbon and hydrogen atoms in the carbon dioxide and water produced by aerobic respiration originally come from?

options.text: From the glucose molecule that is broken down
From the oxygen that is breathed in
options.misconception_tag: thinks the carbon in CO2 comes from inhaled oxygen rather than glucose

options.text: From the carbon dioxide in the air taken into the lungs
options.misconception_tag: thinks CO2 produced is the same CO2 that was breathed in

options.text: From water already inside the cell
options.misconception_tag: thinks the products come from water rather than glucose

stem: In a controlled experiment, germinating peas in a sealed flask cause the surrounding air to become slightly acidic and warmer. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The peas are respiring aerobically, releasing carbon dioxide (which forms an acid in water) and transferring energy as heat
The peas are photosynthesising, releasing oxygen that makes the air acidic
options.misconception_tag: attributes the changes to photosynthesis and thinks oxygen is acidic

options.text: The peas are respiring anaerobically, which is why heat is released
options.misconception_tag: assumes anaerobic respiration because heat is produced, ignoring that the sealed air still contains oxygen

options.text: The peas are taking in carbon dioxide, which makes the flask warmer
options.misconception_tag: thinks CO2 is a reactant taken in during respiration

stem: Which row correctly identifies the reactants AND the products of aerobic respiration?

options.text: Reactants: glucose and oxygen; Products: carbon dioxide and water
Reactants: carbon dioxide and water; Products: glucose and oxygen
options.misconception_tag: swaps respiration reactants and products with photosynthesis

options.text: Reactants: glucose and oxygen; Products: glucose and energy
options.misconception_tag: lists energy and glucose as products, treating energy as a substance and forgetting glucose is used up

options.text: Reactants: glucose only; Products: lactic acid and carbon dioxide
options.misconception_tag: mixes up aerobic with anaerobic respiration and omits oxygen as a reactant

stem: Which word equation correctly represents anaerobic respiration in human muscle cells?

options.text: glucose → lactic acid
glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
options.misconception_tag: confuses anaerobic respiration with aerobic respiration / thinks oxygen is used

options.text: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide
options.misconception_tag: confuses anaerobic respiration in animals with fermentation in yeast

options.text: lactic acid → glucose + oxygen
options.misconception_tag: reverses the reaction / thinks anaerobic respiration builds up glucose

stem: A student claims anaerobic respiration releases MORE energy from a glucose molecule than aerobic respiration. Why is this claim wrong?

options.text: Anaerobic respiration only partially breaks down glucose, so it transfers much LESS energy per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration.
Anaerobic respiration releases more energy, but the energy is lost as heat so it cannot be used.
options.misconception_tag: thinks anaerobic respiration does release more energy but it is wasted

options.text: Anaerobic respiration uses oxygen more efficiently, releasing energy faster but in smaller total amounts.
options.misconception_tag: thinks anaerobic respiration uses oxygen

options.text: Anaerobic respiration releases the same amount of energy, just more slowly.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the energy yield is identical, only the rate differs

stem: Yeast is used to make bread and beer because of the products of its anaerobic respiration. Which products does yeast make?

options.text: Lactic acid only
options.misconception_tag: applies the animal anaerobic pathway to yeast

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water
options.misconception_tag: confuses fermentation products with aerobic respiration products

options.text: Ethanol and carbon dioxide
Ethanol and oxygen
options.misconception_tag: thinks oxygen is a product of respiration rather than a reactant of aerobic respiration

stem: During hard exercise, why do a person's muscles begin to respire anaerobically?

options.text: The muscles cannot get enough oxygen quickly enough to meet the high demand for energy, so they supplement with anaerobic respiration.
The muscles completely stop respiring aerobically the moment exercise begins.
options.misconception_tag: thinks aerobic and anaerobic respiration cannot occur at the same time / aerobic stops entirely

options.text: Anaerobic respiration produces more energy per glucose, which the muscles need during exercise.
options.misconception_tag: thinks anaerobic respiration yields more energy

options.text: Lactic acid produced earlier is now being used as a fuel instead of glucose.
options.misconception_tag: thinks lactic acid is the fuel for anaerobic respiration

stem: Which statement about anaerobic respiration is correct?

options.text: It does not require oxygen, but it is still a form of respiration that transfers energy from glucose.
It is not really respiration because no oxygen is involved.
options.misconception_tag: thinks respiration must involve oxygen to count as respiration

options.text: It releases no energy at all, which is why it is only a backup process.
options.misconception_tag: thinks anaerobic respiration releases no usable energy

options.text: It breaks glucose down completely into carbon dioxide and water without oxygen.
options.misconception_tag: thinks glucose is fully broken down in anaerobic respiration

stem: After a sprint, an athlete continues to breathe deeply and rapidly for several minutes. This is mainly to repay the oxygen debt. What does this extra oxygen do?

options.text: It is used to oxidise the lactic acid that built up, converting it to harmless products.
It is used to convert lactic acid directly back into glucose inside the muscles.
options.misconception_tag: thinks lactic acid is reconverted to glucose in the muscle rather than removed/oxidised

options.text: It replaces the oxygen that was destroyed during anaerobic respiration.
options.misconception_tag: thinks anaerobic respiration consumes or destroys oxygen

options.text: It cools the muscles down after they overheated during exercise.
options.misconception_tag: thinks heavy breathing after exercise is for cooling, not repaying oxygen debt

stem: Where is most of the lactic acid produced by exercising muscles eventually broken down?

options.text: In the lungs
options.misconception_tag: associates lactic acid removal with breathing/lungs because of heavy breathing afterwards

options.text: In the muscles where it was made
options.misconception_tag: thinks lactic acid is dealt with entirely in the muscle, not transported away

options.text: In the liver
In the kidneys, before being excreted in urine
options.misconception_tag: thinks lactic acid is excreted as a waste product rather than broken down in the liver

stem: Respiration reactions are catalysed by enzymes. Which statement about enzymes and anaerobic respiration (fermentation) in plant and yeast cells is correct?

options.text: Respiration reactions are controlled by enzymes, which work whether respiration is aerobic or anaerobic.
Anaerobic respiration needs no enzymes because it is a simpler reaction.
options.misconception_tag: thinks anaerobic respiration is enzyme-free because it is 'simpler'

options.text: Anaerobic respiration only happens in the nucleus, not the cytoplasm.
options.misconception_tag: misplaces the site of respiration / confuses with location of DNA

options.text: Fermentation is not respiration, so it is not controlled by enzymes.
options.misconception_tag: thinks fermentation is separate from respiration

stem: A muscle cell respiring anaerobically uses up glucose. Compared with a muscle cell of the same size respiring aerobically for the same energy output, the anaerobic cell will use:

options.text: More glucose, because each glucose molecule transfers less energy without oxygen.
Less glucose, because anaerobic respiration is more efficient.
options.misconception_tag: thinks anaerobic respiration is more efficient per glucose

options.text: The same amount of glucose, because the energy from one glucose molecule is fixed.
options.misconception_tag: thinks energy yield per glucose is the same regardless of pathway

options.text: No glucose, because anaerobic respiration uses lactic acid as its fuel.
options.misconception_tag: thinks lactic acid, not glucose, is the substrate for anaerobic respiration

stem: Why does anaerobic respiration release less energy per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration?

options.text: Because the glucose is only partially broken down, so much of the chemical energy remains locked in the products (lactic acid or ethanol).
Because some of the glucose is lost as carbon dioxide before it can be respired.
options.misconception_tag: thinks glucose is lost rather than incompletely oxidised

options.text: Because anaerobic respiration happens too fast for the cell to capture the energy.
options.misconception_tag: attributes lower yield to speed rather than incomplete breakdown

options.text: Because anaerobic respiration uses up energy making oxygen for the cell.
options.misconception_tag: thinks the cell makes oxygen during anaerobic respiration

stem: In industry, the anaerobic respiration of yeast is used to produce alcoholic drinks and to make bread rise. Which product is responsible for making bread dough rise?

options.text: Carbon dioxide gas, which forms bubbles in the dough.
Ethanol, which expands the dough as it evaporates.
options.misconception_tag: attributes dough rising to ethanol rather than CO2

options.text: Lactic acid, which produces gas in the dough.
options.misconception_tag: applies animal anaerobic product to yeast and to gas production

options.text: Oxygen, released by the respiring yeast.
options.misconception_tag: thinks respiration releases oxygen

stem: A scientist measures the gases released when yeast is kept in a sealed flask of glucose solution with no air. Which observation best shows the yeast is respiring anaerobically?

options.text: Carbon dioxide is given off, but no oxygen is taken in.
Oxygen is taken in and carbon dioxide is given off.
options.misconception_tag: describes aerobic respiration / thinks anaerobic respiration still takes in oxygen

options.text: No gases are exchanged at all, because there is no oxygen.
options.misconception_tag: thinks without oxygen no gas exchange occurs

options.text: Oxygen is given off as a product of fermentation.
options.misconception_tag: thinks oxygen is produced by respiring yeast

stem: Some bacteria and the cells of a flooded plant root carry out anaerobic respiration. What is the main advantage of being able to respire anaerobically?

options.text: Cells can keep transferring energy from glucose to stay alive even when oxygen is not available.
Cells can release more energy than they would with oxygen, so they grow faster.
options.misconception_tag: thinks anaerobic respiration gives a higher energy yield

options.text: Cells can make their own oxygen so they never run short.
options.misconception_tag: thinks anaerobic respiration generates oxygen for the cell

options.text: Cells avoid producing any waste products, keeping themselves clean.
options.misconception_tag: thinks anaerobic respiration produces no waste products

stem: Which of the following correctly compares aerobic and anaerobic respiration in muscle cells?

options.text: Both transfer energy from glucose, but only aerobic respiration requires oxygen and fully breaks glucose down to carbon dioxide and water.
Both require oxygen, but anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid instead of water.
options.misconception_tag: thinks anaerobic respiration also requires oxygen

options.text: Only anaerobic respiration transfers energy; aerobic respiration is just for gas exchange.
options.misconception_tag: confuses respiration with breathing/gas exchange and misassigns energy transfer

options.text: Both fully break glucose down to carbon dioxide and water, but anaerobic respiration does it without oxygen.
options.misconception_tag: thinks glucose is completely broken down in anaerobic respiration
